interviewQuestions.question: How do you write a code review comment that flags a real problem without making the author defensive?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I aim the comment at the code, not the person, and I make sure it's obvious whether it's blocking or optional.

Concretely, that means: subject is "this function" or "this line," never "you." Instead of "you didn't handle the empty case," I write "what happens here if the list is empty — looks like it'd throw on line 12." Same bug, but one version reads as a judgment of the author and the other reads as two engineers looking at the same code together.

I also mark severity explicitly — `blocking:` for things that must change, `nit:` for cosmetic or optional, `question:` when I'm genuinely unsure and want context I might be missing. Without that marker, an author reading fifteen comments has to guess which three actually gate the merge, and usually either over-corrects everything or has to ask, both of which cost a round trip.

Where it matters, I explain the why, not just the what — "move this to a constant, it's duplicated in three files" teaches something that "move this to a constant" doesn't, and the author is more likely to avoid the pattern next time without me prompting it.

And I try to balance the ledger: if there's a genuinely good decision in the diff, I say so specifically, by name. A review that's only ever critical trains people to dread the notification, and eventually to avoid asking for review at all.

**Testing:** whether you separate technical rigor from tone, or think being right excuses being harsh.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: How do you decide how much effort to put into a review comment, or whether to comment at all?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I calibrate to two things: **blast radius** and **whether the comment is worth the round trip it costs the author**.

For a payment-path change or anything touching auth, I'll spend real time tracing call sites and I won't hesitate to leave several substantive blocking comments, even if that slows the merge — the cost of a bug there is an incident, not an inconvenience.

For a low-stakes internal script or a doc typo fix, I hold myself to a much higher bar before commenting at all, because every comment means the author reads it, decides whether to act, maybe pushes a new commit, and waits for re-review. Five nit comments on a one-line config bump isn't rigor, it's friction with no safety payoff.

The other axis is bikeshedding — I actively check myself for spending effort on the easiest thing to have an opinion about (naming, formatting) while a harder, more important question in the same diff goes unaddressed because it's more work to think through. If a PR has one real architectural risk, that's the comment that has to exist, even if it's the one that takes me the longest to write clearly — and the naming nits can wait or get skipped.

So in short: high-risk code gets deep, direct, even lengthy feedback; low-risk code gets a light touch; and either way, effort goes to the hardest real question in the diff, not the easiest one to comment on.

**Testing:** whether you have an actual calibration model or just review everything at the same fixed depth.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Calibration

interviewQuestions.question: Tell me about a time you had to give feedback on code where the author might have taken it personally. How did you handle it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I don't rely on softening language in the moment to fix this — I try to structure the comment so it can't land as personal in the first place, which mostly means never making the author the grammatical subject of the sentence.

A concrete pattern I use: state the observed behavior, ask what happens under a specific condition, and offer a direction, rather than asserting a verdict. "This is going to break under load, use a queue" becomes "if two requests hit this concurrently, they'd both read the old counter before either writes — I think that double-counts under load. Would a queue or a DB-level atomic increment fix it? Happy to pair if useful."

The last part — offering to pair — matters more than it looks like it should. It reframes the comment from "you got this wrong, fix it" to "we're solving this together," and in practice authors take me up on it more often than I expect, which usually resolves the issue faster than a comment thread would anyway.

When I've gotten this wrong in the past, it's usually been under time pressure — a terse, unmarked, subject-first comment that technically identified the right bug but read as a drive-by criticism. The fix I've settled on is a personal rule: if I'm reviewing quickly, I still spend the extra ten seconds to rephrase as a question before hitting submit.

**Testing:** whether you have a repeatable technique, or just a vague intention to "be nice."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Behavioral

interviewQuestions.question: As a reviewer, how do you avoid bikeshedding — spending all your comments on the easy, low-stakes stuff while a hard design question goes unaddressed?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I treat it as a discipline check I run before I start commenting, not something I trust myself to avoid by instinct, because bikeshedding is seductive precisely because the easy comments are easy to write.

My actual process: I read the whole diff once without commenting, and I ask myself "what's the single riskiest or most important thing in here?" before touching the keyboard. Usually that's a design decision, an edge case, or a performance concern — something that takes real thought to articulate well. I write that comment first, even if it's the slowest one to compose.

Only after that do I go back for naming and style nits, and I deliberately cap how many I leave — if there are more than three or four cosmetic comments, that's usually a sign the diff needs a linter rule added, not fifteen individual comments repeating the same preference.

A concrete example: I once reviewed a PR introducing a new caching layer where the naming was inconsistent throughout, but the real question was whether the cache invalidation strategy handled a specific race condition. It would have been easy to fill the review with naming comments and never get to the race condition, because the naming issues were obvious on first read and the race condition took rereading the code twice to spot. I led with the race condition instead, flagged it as blocking, and left the naming as a single "nit: naming pass would help readability" instead of ten separate comments.

**Testing:** whether you recognize bikeshedding as a real failure mode you actively guard against, or just as a word you've heard.
